strategy:
1. Approach and rationale
Use the supplied discrete construction as a feasible incumbent and locally optimize the same discrete problem at its original resolution. The objective is the maximum of 2n−1 finite-support correlation values, each quadratic in h, so it is nonsmooth and generally nonconvex. Use deterministic multistart SLSQP with analytic gradients: first minimize a sequence of smooth log-sum-exp upper approximations, then polish each resulting feasible point with an exact epigraph formulation of the finite-lag maximum. Keep the best candidate by recomputing the evaluator’s exact score, and never discard a validated parent unless an exactly scored feasible candidate is strictly better.

The log-sum-exp bound and its gradient are exact mathematical facts; SLSQP can handle the stated smooth objectives, box bounds, linear equality, and smooth nonlinear epigraph constraints, but provides only local results here. Continuation and varied starts are heuristics intended to reduce sensitivity to the parent’s basin of attraction. They may improve the construction but do not establish a global optimum or guarantee the target score. Retaining the parent supplies a valid fallback if optimization fails.

2. Mathematical specification
For a length-n real vector h, set dx = 2/n and S = n/2. Require 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 1 for every i and sum_i h[i] = S. Keep the parent’s resolution when it is usable; the default resolution without a parent is n = 42. Do not interpolate or change resolution in the default method.

Represent the evaluator’s 2n−1 finite lags by one zero-lag value and two orientations for each positive distance d. Define
q₀(h) = dx · sum_{i=0}^{n−1} h[i](1−h[i]),
q_d,+(h) = dx · sum_{i=0}^{n−d−1} h[i+d](1−h[i]),
q_d,−(h) = dx · sum_{i=0}^{n−d−1} h[i](1−h[i+d]), for d = 1,…,n−1.
Then the exact discrete objective is C(h) = max of these 2n−1 values. They correspond to every lag of np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode=full), including both lag directions. The shortened index range at nonzero d is essential: it accounts for the partial overlap at the domain boundaries. Do not replace these terms with a full-mass or circular-correlation identity.

For q₀, the gradient component is dx(1−2h[j]). For each d > 0, accumulate the gradients term by term. For q_d,+, each i from 0 through n−d−1 contributes dx(1−h[i]) to component i+d and −dx·h[i+d] to component i. For q_d,−, the same i contributes dx(1−h[i+d]) to component i and −dx·h[i] to component i+d. These rules define one gradient row G_l = ∇q_l for each of the 2n−1 lags and avoid any ambiguous lag-sign convention.

For temperature τ > 0, minimize the smooth upper surrogate φτ(h) = τ log(sum_l exp(q_l(h)/τ)). Evaluate it stably by subtracting qmax = max_l q_l before exponentiation: φτ = qmax + τ log(sum_l exp((q_l−qmax)/τ)). Its gradient is sum_l p_l G_l, where p_l = exp((q_l−qmax)/τ) divided by the sum of those exponentials. It satisfies C(h) ≤ φτ(h) ≤ C(h)+τ log(2n−1). Use this surrogate only to guide search; never return its value as the score.

The exact polishing formulation has decision variables z = (h,t), minimizes t, has 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 1 and t ≥ 0, imposes sum_i h[i] = S, and imposes t−q_l(h) ≥ 0 for every lag l. Its objective gradient is (0,…,0,1), its equality gradient is (1,…,1,0), and the Jacobian row for inequality l is (−G_l,1). This is an exact epigraph representation of C(h), but its quadratic inequalities make the problem nonconvex. SLSQP is used as a local solver, not as a global-optimality certificate.

3. Implementation procedure
1. Write a top-level run(seed=42, **kwargs) and all helper functions at module top level. Use NumPy, math, and scipy.optimize.minimize. Do not define nested helper functions or lambdas, perform file or network I/O, or hard-code or serialize any parent entries. Obtain the optional parent from the runtime global initial_h_values without redefining that global.
2. Validate and determine the dimension. Accept a parent only if it converts to a one-dimensional float array with at least two entries. Its length defines n and takes precedence over any n_points keyword; do not transfer it to a different grid. If a parent has a usable length but nonfinite entries, do not use those entries as a candidate, though its length may define n. With no usable parent, accept an integer kwargs n_points in [2,256], otherwise use 42. A finite parent with entries outside the box or the wrong mass is still usable as a seed after joint feasibility projection. If no parent is usable and its length cannot define n, use the no-parent rule.
3. Implement a top-level lag helper taking h and returning q and G, with q of length M = 2n−1 and G of shape M by n. Use the formulas and slice contributions in section 2, multiply every value and derivative by dx, and include q₀ once only. Implement a separate exact-score helper that returns max(np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode=full)·dx) over the full output. This exact helper, not qmax from an approximate solver variable or a smoothed value, is authoritative for candidate selection and the return value.
4. Implement joint feasibility restoration as a top-level capped-simplex projection helper. For finite input v, find λ such that h[i] = clip(v[i]−λ, 0, 1) and sum_i h[i] = S. This is the Euclidean projection onto the box with the required mass; it is not successive clipping and rescaling. Find λ by bisection on [min(v)−1, max(v)]: the lower endpoint clips every entry to 1 and the upper endpoint clips every entry to 0. At each of 80 iterations, if the clipped sum exceeds S, move the lower endpoint to the midpoint; otherwise move the upper endpoint. Form h using the final midpoint. Reject nonfinite v; for overflow protection, bound finite projection inputs to a safe magnitude such as 10^6 before bisection.
5. Correct bisection roundoff without violating the box. Compute the residual S−sum(h) using math.fsum, add a positive residual only into available 1−h[i] capacity or remove a negative residual only from available h[i] capacity, and recompute after each adjustment. Then, if needed, choose an interior coordinate j and set it to S minus the stable sum of all other entries, provided the result is in [0,1]. Check both the float64 NumPy sum and the stable sum; require bounds exactly and mass error at most 1e−10. If correction cannot produce a valid vector, use the constant vector h[i]=0.5, which is feasible for the supported dimensions. Apply this same helper to parent repairs, starts, and optimizer outputs.
6. Establish a valid incumbent before any solver call. If the parent is finite, use it directly as the first seed; if it is already within the box and has the required mass, preserve it except for a roundoff-scale mass correction. Otherwise project it jointly. Compute its exact score and retain this feasible parent-derived vector as fallback. Always also establish the constant 0.5 fallback and its exact score. If no valid parent exists, use the constant vector as the initial incumbent.
7. Build a deterministic, deduplicated start list using rng = np.random.default_rng(seed). With a usable parent, include the parent seed, three projected perturbations parent + σ·normal with σ in {0.10, 0.25, 0.50}, a block vector, an alternating vector, and two independent uniform random vectors projected to the mass constraint. Without a usable parent, include the constant vector, the block vector, the alternating vector, one sinusoid 0.5 + 0.45 sin(2πi/n), and four independent uniform random vectors. Construct the block vector with floor(n/2) leading ones, zeros elsewhere, and a 0.5 at the next position when n is odd. Construct the alternating vector algorithmically from i mod 2. Project every non-parent pattern and perturbation; remove starts whose maximum coordinate difference from an earlier start is below 1e−10. These are starts, not feasibility relaxations.
8. For each start, first project it and compute its exact score. Then run four continuation stages with τ = 0.02, 0.005, 0.001, and 0.0002. For each stage call scipy.optimize.minimize with method SLSQP, the top-level soft objective returning both value and analytic gradient, jac=True, bounds [0,1] on all h entries, and the single equality sum(h)−S = 0 with an all-ones Jacobian. Use ftol = 1e−10 and maxiter = 120. Warm-start each stage from the accepted point of the preceding stage. If a result has a finite vector of the expected shape, project it, evaluate its exact score for the global incumbent, and compare its φτ with the current point. Advance that start only when the projected point’s φτ is no greater than the current value plus 1e−12. If the solver raises an exception or returns unusable data, retain the prior point and continue to the next temperature. Do not rely solely on the solver success flag.
9. After the four smooth stages for each start, run exact epigraph polishing from that start’s current feasible point. Set its initial t to max_l q_l(h) plus max(1e−8, 1e−6·abs(max_l q_l(h))). Use the decision vector (h,t), bounds [0,1] on h and [0,∞) on t, the linear mass equality, and the vector inequality t−q_l(h) ≥ 0 for all M lags. Supply the objective, equality, and inequality Jacobians specified in section 2 as top-level callbacks. Use SLSQP with ftol = 1e−10 and maxiter = 200. If the returned decision vector is finite and correctly shaped, project its h part and compare that feasible h by exact score; the returned t is never the reported score. A failed status is not itself a reason to discard a finite candidate. Catch solver exceptions and keep the incumbent. After all starts, perform one more epigraph polish from the global exact-score incumbent.
10. Maintain one global best feasible vector and its exact score. Record any projected candidate only if it passes finite, dimension, box, and mass checks and its exact score is lower than the incumbent by more than 1e−12; this tie rule preserves the parent when there is no material improvement. Independently of whether a candidate becomes the global best, keep the per-start continuation point only under the smooth-value rule in step 8. Before returning, restore feasibility once more, validate it, and recompute the exact score from the final vector. If this final check fails, return the constant 0.5 vector and its recomputed exact score. Return exactly (h_values as a NumPy array, c5_bound as a Python float, n_points as an integer).

4. Search choices and useful variations
Use the defaults in section 3: parent resolution or n=42, eight starts, four temperatures, 120 SLSQP iterations per smooth stage, and 200 per epigraph solve. Keep all starts and solver calls sequential on the available single CPU. The exact score, exact mass constraint, box constraint, parent fallback, and final epigraph polish are correctness requirements, not tuning options.

The meaningful static variations are the number and diversity of starts, the temperatures, and how many distinct points receive epigraph polishing. If a smaller source/runtime variant is desired, use six starts and polish only the best three distinct smooth-stage candidates by exact score; otherwise use the default eight and polish every start plus the final incumbent. A reasonable temperature schedule has three to five decreasing values, starts near 0.01–0.05 and ends near 0.0001–0.0005; retain an exact epigraph stage regardless of the final temperature. Parent perturbation standard deviations between 0.08 and 0.6 are practical, with the specified three scales as the default. These are local-search heuristics; choose settings statically rather than asking the program author to measure or tune them. Always keep deterministic seeding and select the final result by the exact evaluator score.

5. Numerical robustness and memory use
For the supplied parent n=42, M=83 and G has only 83·42 float entries, about 28 kB in float64. The lag-gradient work is quadratic in n per evaluation but uses only the M-by-n gradient matrix, not a three-dimensional array or a dense Hessian. With no parent, cap optional n_points at 256; if a supplied parent has n>256, retain or jointly repair and score its fallback but skip the multistart nonlinear search to bound single-CPU cost. Score computation still uses the exact full correlation. Do not parallelize or allocate a larger-resolution representation.

Use float64 throughout. The shifted log-sum-exp prevents exponential overflow; underflow of nonmaximal terms is harmless because at least one shifted exponential equals one. Reject nonfinite solver results before projection or scoring. The projection bracket and residual correction enforce feasibility jointly; never use a clip-then-rescale repair. Keep a previously validated incumbent if SLSQP fails, stops early, or produces an invalid vector. Each optimizer call ends by its SLSQP convergence rule or fixed iteration cap, and the finite start list ends the overall search. The method is local and no result should be described as globally optimal.

6. Runtime safeguards and return contract
The generated program must perform all input checks and calculations when the harness later calls run(). It must check the parent shape and finite values, derive n from the parent when usable, enforce 0≤h[i]≤1 and sum(h)=n/2 through the capped-simplex projection, and validate every stored candidate before scoring it. It must implement the exact score as the maximum of the full np.correlate(h, 1−h, mode=full) output multiplied by 2/n, including every lag and both directions. Do not return a log-sum-exp objective, an epigraph t, or a score computed from a different boundary convention.

Initialize a valid fallback before entering solver code so import, callback, or solver exceptions cannot leave run without an answer. Preserve a validated parent as the incumbent unless a feasible candidate has a strictly lower exact score under the stated comparison rule. If no usable parent or solver candidate exists, return the feasible constant 0.5 construction. Recheck the final vector, repair only through the joint feasibility helper, recompute its exact score, and return the required three-tuple with matching vector length and n_points. Do not claim that the generated program has run or that it reaches the target; its source must implement the search and all fallback operations for the harness to execute.
